clarifyingQuestions: Can task IDs repeat, or should a later add replace an earlier task?
Should expiration be based on enqueue time or `run_at` time?
Should priority be higher-is-better or lower-is-better?
followUps: Support updating priority for an existing task.
Separate waiting tasks from ready tasks for better performance.
followUpGuide: For cancellation, first decide whether cancel(task_id) removes every pending entry with that ID or just one entry. Use unique entry IDs for per-entry cancellation. A permanent canceled-ID set would also reject future adds with that ID; use generations if re-adding should be allowed.

For updates, identify the entry to update because task IDs can repeat. Push a new version with an incremented generation number and retain the chosen tie-order policy. The pop path skips stale generations.
For scale, maintain one heap ordered by `run_at` and another ready heap ordered by priority. Move due tasks from waiting to ready before popping.
complexityAnalysis: - List scan approach (shipped guide): Time: O(1) amortized per add and O(n) per pop, where n is the stored entry count. Space: O(n), including temporary candidate/filter lists.

- Single priority heap: Time: O(log n) per add, but a future high-priority head cannot be discarded. Inspecting and reinserting future entries can cost O(n log n) per pop repeatedly; there is no general O(log n) amortized pop bound.

- Dual waiting/ready heaps (follow-up): Time: O(log n) per add; a pop promoting k newly due entries and discarding s expired ready heads costs O((k + s + 1) log n). Each entry is promoted and removed at most once, giving O(log n) amortized work per entry plus O(1) per empty poll. Space: O(n). Lazy cancellation adds stale-entry removals.
solutionGuide: One simple solution stores all tasks in a list and scans for due candidates on `pop`. For interview clarity, that's acceptable if constraints are small.
The important behavior is semantic: not-yet-due tasks can't be returned, expired tasks are removed, and priority ties keep insertion order.
def add(self, task_id, priority: int, run_at: float = 0, ttl: float | None = None) -> None:
return task["ttl"] is not None and now >= task["run_at"] + task["ttl"]
self.tasks = [task for task in self.tasks if not self._expired(task, now)]
candidates = [task for task in self.tasks if task["run_at"] <= now]
If asked to optimize, replace the scan with separate waiting and ready heaps.
